title: Live-mode WriteDetail silently drops replaceIndex — every 'replace' becomes 'append' on Windows, sim says success
userOrOpsImpact: Operator says 'fix the typo in row 3 of JOHNS's W-2s — the employer name should be ACME not ACMA'. LLM calls lacerte_detail_write(replaceIndex: 2, ...). In sim it works — row 2 is replaced and the test passes. In live (Windows + Lacerte), the bridge call drops replaceIndex on the floor: it has no replaceIndex parameter at all (Writer.WriteDetail(appId, dataPath, clientNumber, row) takes a 4-arg signature, lines 146-181), and the session-manager live branch literally writes '_ = replaceIndex;' twice (lines 1199, 1205). The SDK gets an APPEND call, the wrong row stays, and a duplicate row is added. The tool returns statusCode=1 Success and the LLM reports the fix landed. Two-mode discipline ('sim and live observationally identical') broken on the exact path an operator uses to undo a data-entry mistake.
description: DetailsTools.LacerteDetailWrite exposes replaceIndex with description 'Optional zero-based index to overwrite an existing row instead of appending.' The session manager honors it in sim (ApplySimDetailWriteWithUndo, line 1220) and SimulationStore.WriteDetail performs `list[replaceIndex.Value] = row` with an OutOfIndex throw for invalid indices. The live branch at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1187-1210 ignores replaceIndex entirely — both `_ = replaceIndex;` discards (lines 1199 and 1205) and the bridge call `_bridge.WriteDetail(appId, ctx.DataPath, clientNumber, row)` doesn't accept it. The bridge Writer.WriteDetail at Writer.cs:146 has no replaceIndex parameter. So a live replace silently becomes a live append; the tool's response envelope echoes the operator-supplied replaceIndex back as if it were honored.
recommendation: Two-part fix. (1) Until the live path can honor replaceIndex (SDK's WriteToDetailFile only appends per spec §2; true replace would need a delete+append or undocumented update), make the tool layer fail-CLOSED in live mode when replaceIndex is supplied: in DetailsTools.LacerteDetailWrite or the session WriteDetail, if Mode==Live && replaceIndex.HasValue throw a new SyntheticStatusCode like 9019 LiveReplaceIndexUnsupported with remediation 'Detail-row replace-by-index is not supported on live SDK paths in v0.1 — read the existing rows via lacerte_detail_read, write a fresh append, and delete the old row via the upcoming lacerte_detail_delete tool.' Better than silent corruption. (2) Add a regression test under Parity/ that exercises the both-modes contract: write a row, then attempt a replace at the appended row's index, then assert that BOTH modes produce the same observable outcome (either both replace OR both throw the same error). Today no such test exists — DetailWriteRoundTripTests only runs in sim. (3) Update DECISIONS.md to log that replace-by-index is sim-only in v0.1 and document the live escape hatch when implemented.
rationale: Prior rounds covered replaceIndex ergonomics (P16-008 detail-write param defaults), prompt shapes (P16-017), and casing (P16-080). None examined the live-vs-sim divergence on replaceIndex. The two `_ = replaceIndex;` discards are unmistakable evidence the live path knowingly drops the parameter. Cost-of-failure lens specifically asked 'Replace-by-index semantics — clear from the operator's seat?' — operator sees 'replace' in the tool description, gets 'append' in live with statusCode=Success. That is the textbook fail-OPEN posture this lens hunts.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct read. LacerteSessionManager.cs lines 1199 and 1205 contain literal `_ = replaceIndex;` discards in both the dryRun and non-dryRun branches of the live path. The live bridge call at line 1207-1208 is `_bridge.WriteDetail(appId, ctx.DataPath, ctx.Year, ctx.Module, clientNumber, row)` — replaceIndex is not passed. Bridge/Writer.cs:146-181 confirms the static `WriteDetail(string appId, string dataPath, string clientNumber, DetailRow row)` signature has no replaceIndex parameter (the underlying COM call is WriteToDetailFile, which per spec §2 only appends). The sim path at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1620-1646 (ApplySimDetailWriteWithUndo) properly honors replaceIndex with `list[i] = row` and an OutOfIndex throw for invalid indices. So sim does replace, live silently appends — the textbook fail-OPEN posture this audit ground rule (CLAUDE.md two-mode discipline) explicitly forbids.

Novelty check across all three audit-findings files: P16-008 covers detail-write param-defaults (ergonomics, not semantics), P16-017 covers the WorkflowPrompts.cs nested-row shape bug (call shape, not divergence), P16-080 covers ALL-CAPS parameter casing (clientID vs clientId), P15-011 added DetailWriteRoundTripTests but that test is sim-only and never crosses the live boundary. R1's WriteDetail-area findings (#600/602 list-locking, #930s perf) cover concurrency and dry-run cost — not the live silent-drop. The two `_ = replaceIndex;` discards are unmistakable evidence the live path knowingly throws away the parameter, and no prior round flagged this. Genuinely new.

Material improvement: this is a data-correction path (operator says "fix the typo in row 3 of JOHNS's W-2s"). In live mode the SDK gets an APPEND, the wrong row stays, a duplicate row is added, and the tool returns statusCode=1 Success — the LLM reports success and the operator believes the typo is fixed. This is the exact failure mode the project's two-mode discipline exists to prevent. The fail-CLOSED fix (throw a new SyntheticStatusCode 9019 LiveReplaceIndexUnsupported when Mode==Live && replaceIndex.HasValue) is ~15-20 LOC in DetailsTools or the session manager, plus a small parity test under Parity/. The recommendation correctly notes the SDK has no true replace path in v0.1 — so fail-closed with a documented escape hatch (read+append+delete once a delete tool ships) is the right posture. Caveat: the live path is currently "Live verification deferred to Windows + Lacerte box" per the code comments, so the bug only bites once live mode is actually exercised — but the moment a Windows box runs lacerte_detail_write with replaceIndex set, real W-2/1099 data gets corrupted with the tool reporting success. Landing the gate now (before first live use) is materially cheaper than discovering it during live verification. High-signal finding worth landing.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two-part fix, ~30 min of work, all sim-testable off-Windows except step (3):

(1) Fail-CLOSED at the tool layer for live-mode replaceIndex. Add a new SyntheticStatusCode in src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/SyntheticStatusCodes.cs:
```
public const int LiveReplaceIndexUnsupported = 9019;
// Remediation: "Detail-row replace-by-index is not supported on the live Lacerte SDK
//  path in v0.1 — the SDK's WriteToDetailFile only appends. To correct a row in live
//  mode, read the existing rows via lacerte_detail_read, write a fresh appended row
//  with the correction, and delete the stale row via lacerte_detail_delete (P-future).
//  This guard prevents silent data divergence between sim and live."
```
Wire it in src/LacertMCP.Server/Session/LacerteSessionManager.cs:1187 — at the top of the Mode==Live branch, before the dryRun split, add:
```
if (replaceIndex.HasValue)
{
    throw new LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.LiveReplaceIndexUnsupported,
        new Dictionary<string, object?>
        {
            ["replaceIndex"] = replaceIndex.Value,
            ["clientNumber"] = clientNumber,
            ["op"] = "WriteDetail"
        });
}
```
This makes the two `_ = replaceIndex;` discards dead code — remove both lines (1199 and 1205) as part of the same edit so the next reader doesn't think replaceIndex is silently honored.

(2) Add a Parity test at src/LacertMCP.Tests/Parity/WriteDetailReplaceIndexParityTests.cs that exercises both modes' replaceIndex behavior and asserts they fail or succeed identically. Use SimulationStore for sim and a mock IBridgeClient that captures the WriteDetail call args for live. The test should:
  - In sim: write a row, then attempt a replace at the appended row's index, then read back and assert the row was replaced (not appended).
  - In live (mocked): write a row, then attempt a replace at the appended row's index, then assert the tool throws LacerteSDKError(9019) BEFORE the bridge.WriteDetail is invoked (i.e., the mock never receives a second call).
  - Cross-mode assertion: BOTH modes either honor replaceIndex with replace semantics OR both fail with the same observable error — never one silently appends while the other replaces. This is the two-mode-discipline contract.
The test class belongs under Parity/ alongside the existing parity tests, not under Tools/ — its purpose is to lock in the sim-live observational identity invariant.

(3) Add a DECISIONS.md entry dated today:
```
## 2026-06-04 — Detail-row replace-by-index is sim-only in v0.1

The Lacerte SDK's WriteToDetailFile COM method only appends; there is no
documented update-by-index path. Rather than silently drop replaceIndex on the
live wire (the prior behavior, two `_ = replaceIndex;` discards at
LacerteSessionManager.cs:1199/1205), we fail-CLOSED with synthetic status
9019 LiveReplaceIndexUnsupported whenever Mode==Live && replaceIndex.HasValue.
Sim continues to honor replaceIndex with full replace semantics (used by tests
and by the in-memory operator workflow). When lacerte_detail_delete lands
(P-future), the live escape hatch becomes read+append+delete; revisit this
decision then.
```
Also update REQUIREMENTS.md (or ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md if that's where tool-surface contracts live) to note that lacerte_detail_write's replaceIndex parameter is sim-only in v0.1.

(4) Update the [Description] string on the replaceIndex parameter in DetailsTools.LacerteDetailWrite to say: "Optional zero-based index to overwrite an existing row instead of appending. **Sim mode only in v0.1** — supplying this in live mode returns synthetic status 9019. Use lacerte_detail_read + lacerte_detail_delete + append for live row corrections." This makes the constraint visible at the tool catalog level so the LLM doesn't try and discover the limitation by trial and error.

Net diff: ~50 LOC across 5 files (SyntheticStatusCodes.cs, LacerteSessionManager.cs, DetailsTools.cs, new Parity test, DECISIONS.md/REQUIREMENTS.md). Zero Windows dependency for landing the gate + test; live verification of the 9019 throw is straightforward once the Windows box is available.

title: Live-mode WriteField bypasses the table-3/4 stateAbbrev + table-2/4 subClientId discriminator gates that sim enforces
userOrOpsImpact: Operator runs a bulk state-tax sweep across 200 clients via lacerte_field_write_bulk with table=3 but forgets stateAbbrev on a few entries (or the LLM omits it because the column was blank in the spreadsheet). In sim this is rejected per-row with 9011 StateAbbrevRequired — the operator sees the bad rows and fixes them. In live, the same call passes BridgeInputValidation (which allows null/empty stateAbbrev) and the session manager calls _bridge.UpdateTaxReturn(..., stateAbbrev ?? string.Empty) — handing an empty string to the SDK for a STATE table write. Best case the SDK rejects with a less-actionable error; worst case the SDK applies the write to a default/sentinel state row (or the first state row alphabetically), silently mutating the wrong return. Same hazard with subClientId for tables 2 and 4 (sim throws SubClientIDRequired; live passes subClientId ?? 0).
description: ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo at lines 1549-1565 has explicit per-table discriminator gates: table==2 requires subClientId>0 (else 9010), table==3 requires non-empty stateAbbrev (else 9011), table==4 requires both. The live branch (1063-1113) goes straight from access-map check to `_bridge.UpdateTaxReturn(appId, ctx.DataPath, ctx.Year, ctx.Module, table, clientNumber, field, value, subClientId, stateAbbrev)`. Writer.UpdateTaxReturn at Bridge/Writer.cs:90 does its own validation via ValidateUpdateTaxReturnArgs, but that validator (BridgeInputValidation.cs:487-511) checks only subClientId>=0 and stateAbbrev shape (when non-empty) — it has no table-aware required-field gate. The downstream `subClientId ?? 0` and `stateAbbrev ?? string.Empty` coercions at Writer.cs:110 then hand zero/empty to the SDK for tables that semantically require them.
recommendation: Hoist the discriminator gate out of ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo into the WriteField chokepoint so it runs BEFORE the Mode==Live branch (and gets inherited by ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo for free). Concretely: in LacerteSessionManager.WriteField after `RejectIfReadOnly` and before `ExecuteWithIdempotencyLock`, add: `if ((table == 2 || table == 4) && (!subClientId.HasValue || subClientId.Value <= 0)) throw new LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.SubClientIDRequired);` and `if ((table == 3 || table == 4) && string.IsNullOrEmpty(stateAbbrev)) throw new LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.StateAbbrevRequired);`. Remove the now-redundant copies from ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo. Add a parity test under Parity/WriteParityTests that asserts both modes throw the same code on a table-3 write without stateAbbrev. While there, also tighten ValidateUpdateTaxReturnArgs to accept a `table` parameter and apply the same gate as defense-in-depth.
rationale: Prior rounds added DATA6/DATA7 read-only gates (P14-054), access-map fail-closed (P14-024), DryRun undo (P14-043), and bridge-input validation (P14-050). None hoisted the per-table discriminator gates to the live path. The two-mode discipline in CLAUDE.md is the load-bearing invariant this finding pins down — and a state-sweep over 200 clients is exactly the operator scenario REQUIREMENTS §1.2 names. Sim's gate evidently exists because the validation IS necessary; live silently elides it. Fix is ~10 lines, sim-testable, no Windows or SDK access needed.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified all factual claims by direct file reads:

(1) LacerteSessionManager.cs:1063-1113 — the live branch confirmed to call `_bridge.UpdateTaxReturn(appId, ctx.DataPath, ctx.Year, ctx.Module, table, clientNumber, field, value, subClientId, stateAbbrev)` directly after `FieldAccessMapLoader.AssertWritable` at line 1048 with NO table-discriminator gate. The only pre-bridge validations are: access-map check, idempotency cache lookup, and `RejectIfReadOnly` (much earlier). No `if (table == 2 ...)` / `if (table == 3 ...)` check exists on the live path.

(2) LacerteSessionManager.cs:1549-1565 — confirmed `ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo` has explicit per-table discriminator gates: case 2 throws `SubClientIDRequired` on missing/<=0 subClientID; case 3 throws `StateAbbrevRequired` on empty stateAbbrev; case 4 throws both. These are sim-only — the live branch at 1063-1113 never enters this method.

(3) Bridge/BridgeInputValidation.cs:487-511 — confirmed `ValidateUpdateTaxReturnArgs` checks only `subClientId.HasValue && subClientId.Value < 0` (accepts 0!) and `ValidateStateAbbrev(stateAbbrev, op)` which accepts null/empty per its name (no table parameter, no table-aware gate).

(4) Bridge/Writer.cs:108-111 — confirmed the coercion `subClientId ?? 0, stateAbbrev ?? string.Empty` sends sentinel values straight to the SDK COM call when the operator omits them on a table-2/3/4 write.

(5) Grep across the entire server confirms `SubClientIDRequired` and `StateAbbrevRequired` are referenced ONLY in SyntheticStatusCodes.cs (definition) and LacerteSessionManager.cs:1551-1563 (the sim-only gate). The live path never throws these codes.

(6) `table == 2|3|4` discriminator-gate pattern exists ONLY in SimulationStore.cs:305-309 (a separate sim lookup path) and the sim ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo. The live path has zero matches.

Novelty check against prior 234 findings: grepped audit-findings.json + r2 + r3 for stateAbbrev/SubClientIDRequired/StateAbbrevRequired/discriminator/live bypass/ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo. Prior round hits cluster around:
- Naming inconsistency `stateAbbr` vs `stateAbbrev` (r3 P16-ish, audit-findings.json #1103) — cosmetic API consistency
- Bridge-boundary validation (P14-050, P15-020) — added validator but no table-aware gate
- Lowercase normalization at read tools (r3) — different path/code
- ClientID case-normalization (r3 P16-038) — different field

NONE of the prior findings target the specific sim/live divergence where ApplySimFieldWriteWithUndo's per-table discriminator gates fail to fire on the live path. This is genuinely novel.

Materiality: The finding pins down the load-bearing CLAUDE.md two-mode invariant ("Simulation and live must be observationally identical for the happy path"). REQUIREMENTS §1.2 explicitly names bulk state-tax sweeps across hundreds of clients as a P0 operator scenario, exactly the scenario where stateAbbrev omission is most likely. The behavior divergence:
- Sim: per-row 9011 StateAbbrevRequired with clear remediation
- Live: empty-string stateAbbrev forwarded to SDK; best case opaque rejection, worst case silent wrong-state write (data corruption on a tax return)

This is data-corruption-class risk, not hygiene. Fix is ~10 LOC, sim-testable via Parity/WriteParityTests, no Windows or SDK access needed.

title: Heartbeat payload omits ExpiresAt/MinutesUntilExpiry/buildVersion — README explicitly advertises 'auth countdown, build version' that the file never contains; watcher sees registered:true for hours after the 24h ticket has actually expired
userOrOpsImpact: An operator who runs the MCP server unattended (the exact use case the heartbeat was built for in P15-054) sets up a PowerShell watcher per the README guidance. README.md:154 documents the heartbeat JSON as containing '(pid, mode, auth countdown, build version)'. The actual payload built in BuildPayload() is `{pid, registered, mode, ts}` — no `expiresAt`, no `minutesUntilExpiry`, no `buildVersion`. Worse: the `registered` boolean reflects the in-memory IsRegistered latch, which is NOT updated when the 24h Intuit ticket lapses — IsRegistered only flips to false inside ThrowIfAuthExpired which fires on the NEXT tool call. So if the server sits idle from 11pm to 9am with a ticket that expired at 2am, the heartbeat keeps writing `registered:true` every 30 seconds until 9am's first tool call. The watcher sees green, the operator wakes up, runs a read, gets LoginExpired (9007), and now distrusts the heartbeat for the rest of the engagement. This defeats the entire purpose of P15-054's 'closes the auth-quietly-expired-6-hours-ago failure mode' justification.
description: Three coupled gaps. (1) HeartbeatWriter.BuildPayload (line 155-162) hard-codes only {pid, registered, mode, ts} — the SessionStatusSnapshot at LacerteSessionManager.cs:453-479 carries ExpiresAt, MinutesUntilExpiry, BuildVersion, ModeResolutionReason and the heartbeat could just project from it. (2) README.md:154 already publishes the richer schema as fact, so this is a docs-vs-code drift in addition to a real ops gap. (3) `registered` is read from _session.IsRegistered which lags real ticket state by up-to-N-hours because the proactive ThrowIfAuthExpired probe only runs at tool-call entry through RequireContext. A watcher that polls only the heartbeat sees a stale green light. r3 P16-033 added the README documentation but never reconciled with the actual writer; r2 P15-054 built the writer with a minimal payload and never expanded it. No prior round caught this end-to-end gap.
recommendation: In HeartbeatWriter.BuildPayload, project from `_session.SessionStatus()` (the existing snapshot) rather than reading IsRegistered + Mode in isolation. New payload: `{pid, mode, registered, expiresAt:ISO, minutesUntilExpiry, buildVersion, ts}`. Critically, compute `registered` as `IsRegistered && ExpiresAt.HasValue && ExpiresAt.Value > DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` so the heartbeat truthfully flips to false at the moment the ticket expires, independent of whether a tool call has fired since. Add a test that pins ExpiresAt 1 second in the past via SetExpiresAtForTest and asserts the heartbeat payload returns `registered:false`. The single line that today reads `registered = _session.IsRegistered` is the bug; the snapshot already does the right math at LacerteSessionManager.cs:430-434.
rationale: r2 P15-054 shipped HeartbeatWriter with the minimal {pid, registered, mode, ts} payload. r3 P16-033 noticed the env var wasn't in README and added a README row whose example schema described the richer shape (auth countdown, build version) — but no audit round read the BuildPayload code against that doc to catch the lie. The IsRegistered staleness across an idle window is a separate concern none of the 234 prior findings addressed. Confirmed by reading lines 149-163 of HeartbeatWriter.cs and lines 453-479 of LacerteSessionManager.cs.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified all three claims by direct file read.

(1) HeartbeatWriter.BuildPayload at C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Diagnostics/HeartbeatWriter.cs:149-163 emits exactly {pid, registered, mode, ts} — the doc comment at lines 23 and 151-154 even pins this as the intentional schema ('Keep the schema small and stable — {pid, registered, mode, ts} is the task-level contract; we add nothing beyond it here'). No expiresAt, no minutesUntilExpiry, no buildVersion.

(2) README.md:154 reads `(pid, mode, auth countdown, build version)` — a 4-field schema where 'auth countdown' and 'build version' are NOT in the actual payload. Real doc-vs-code drift. Confirmed via grep -i.

(3) Staleness verified by grep on IsRegistered/ExpiresAt/ThrowIfAuthExpired in LacerteSessionManager.cs: IsRegistered is only ever flipped to false inside ThrowIfAuthExpired() at line 1423-1427, which fires from RequireContext (line 1387) which only runs at tool-call entry. The heartbeat at HeartbeatWriter.cs:158 reads `_session.IsRegistered` raw — so an idle server with a 24h Intuit ticket that lapsed at 2am keeps writing `registered:true` every 30s until the next tool call. SessionStatus() at line 427-479 already does the right math (line 430-434 derives minutesUntilExpiry) — the heartbeat could just project from the existing snapshot. The required test seam SetExpiresAtForTest already exists at line 1994.

Novelty check across all three audit files: r1 has zero hits for heartbeat/HeartbeatWriter. r2 has #803 (P15-033 area) which added README env-var ROWS but did not specify payload schema or check ExpiresAt staleness; r2 #1503 covered SessionMode casing only. r3 P16-033 added the line 154 README row with the richer wording ('auth countdown, build version') without reconciling against BuildPayload — that's the proximate cause of the doc-code drift, and no audit round caught it. r3 P16-061/P16-062 again only touched mode-casing. r3 #1628 surfaced DebugWireEnabled/WireLogPath on SessionStatus (different surface). None addresses the end-to-end gap: payload omits the three fields the README advertises AND the registered bit lies during idle windows.

Materially improves: Yes. The whole reason P15-054 added the writer (per its own xmldoc lines 24-26) was 'Closes the operator runs the MCP unattended and never notices the 24h Intuit auth quietly expired 6 hours ago failure mode the audit flagged.' Today, on an idle server, the heartbeat keeps the green light on for that exact window. Fix is small (project from SessionStatus snapshot + compute `registered = IsRegistered && ExpiresAt > UtcNow`) and curative. This is not bikeshedding — it directly undoes the value of an existing audit fix.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Replace HeartbeatWriter.BuildPayload (HeartbeatWriter.cs:149-163) to project from _session.SessionStatus(). New payload: `{pid, mode, registered, expiresAt, minutesUntilExpiry, buildVersion, ts}` where `registered = snapshot.IsRegistered && snapshot.ExpiresAt.HasValue && snapshot.ExpiresAt.Value > DateTimeOffset.UtcNow`. Emit `expiresAt` as ISO-8601 (`o`) and `minutesUntilExpiry` as the snapshot value (already clamped >= 0 at LacerteSessionManager.cs:432-433). Use the same lowercase `mode` already in place to preserve the r3 P16-061/P16-062 casing contract. Update the line 152-154 doc comment in BuildPayload to match the new schema. Add a unit test in src/LacertMCP.Tests that: (a) calls SetExpiresAtForTest with `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.AddSeconds(-1)`, runs TryWrite, asserts the parsed payload has `registered:false` and `minutesUntilExpiry:0` even though IsRegistered backing field is still true (no tool call has fired); (b) asserts buildVersion, expiresAt are populated. Optional: add a corresponding parity test asserting README.md:154 documents exactly the field set BuildPayload emits, to prevent the next drift. No README change needed beyond verifying line 154's enumeration matches the new payload (it already does).

title: Idempotency cache is purely in-memory — any process restart (MCP host crash, Claude Desktop reload, OS update reboot mid-batch) silently un-fingerprints every prior write so the LLM's retry replays the same write against the live tax return
userOrOpsImpact: Realistic scenario: operator's LLM is mid-way through a 30-call batch update (e.g., 'set W-2 box 1 on these 30 returns'), each call carries the LLM-generated idempotencyKey 'batch-2026-06-04-w2-cn1001..1030' per the workflow that the README explicitly recommends. Call 15 lands, then Claude Desktop is updated/restarted (or the operator's box pulls down a Windows update and reboots), which kills the MCP child process. On reload, the LLM (which has no memory of which calls landed because it was reloaded too OR re-prompted from a fresh chat) re-issues calls 1-30 with the same idempotencyKeys, expecting the 9102 IdempotencyConflict (cached) replay path to no-op the 15 that already landed. Instead, `_idempotencyCache = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, IdempotencyCacheEntry>()` is freshly empty after the restart, all 30 calls miss the cache, and the 15 already-applied writes execute a SECOND time against the live SDK — overwriting any human corrections, doubling detail-row appends (WriteDetail without replaceIndex APPENDS), and silently re-incrementing CreateClient row counters. Worse, the second execution gets cached, so a THIRD retry would correctly replay — but the damage is done. The 24h IdempotencyTtl that suggests durability is doubly misleading: it's wall-clock 24h from process-start, not from key-issuance, so a restart 23h59m into a batch resets it to zero with no warning. There is no persistence layer, no on-disk shadow log, and the heartbeat doesn't surface 'cache cleared at startup' so an operator/LLM can't know to skip retry.
description: _idempotencyCache and _idempotencyLocks are both `new ConcurrentDictionary<...>()` instance fields with no serialization, no on-disk shadow log, no startup-restore. Dispose at line 2158-2169 just disposes semaphores; nothing flushes. README mentions idempotency keys as the canonical retry-safety mechanism but doesn't disclose the cache is process-volatile. The result: idempotency is honored WITHIN a single process lifetime but offers ZERO protection across the most common restart scenarios (MCP host restart, OS reboot, server crash, manual Ctrl+C, Claude Desktop update install). The danger is asymmetric: WriteField is idempotent in the SDK sense (same field, same value, same effect), but WriteDetail without replaceIndex APPENDS (so re-execution doubles), and CreateClient mints a NEW ClientNumber on every miss (so re-execution creates a duplicate client with a new number — the SDK would reject the ClientID collision with DuplicateClient(8) but only IF the operator passed the same ClientID; an LLM that generated 'client-{i}' style IDs and is now confused about which i's landed will happily mint new client records).
recommendation: Two graduated options, pick at least (a): (a) MINIMUM — on the first TryReplayIdempotent miss after process start, emit ONE structured warning to the wire log AND include an `idempotencyCacheColdStart: true` flag on the next N tool envelopes' context (or expose it on SessionStatus + the heartbeat) so the LLM/operator can SEE that cache state was lost and pause for confirmation before retry. This is ~30 lines and prevents silent corruption. (b) PROPER — persist (key, payloadFingerprint, result, createdAt) to `%LOCALAPPDATA%/LacertMCP/idempotency.jsonl` on StoreIdempotent (append-only, line-delimited, easy to truncate on TTL prune) and load on ctor. Crash-safe because each write is one fsync'd line; a torn last line is skipped via try/parse. Lives behind LACERTE_IDEMPOTENCY_PERSIST=1 to stay opt-in until validated. Also document the cache volatility in README's idempotency section: 'Idempotency keys protect against in-process retry; on server restart the cache is empty and a retry of an already-applied write WILL re-execute against the live SDK. Enable LACERTE_IDEMPOTENCY_PERSIST=1 for cross-restart protection.'
rationale: r1 P14-013/P14-064 and r2 P15-041/P15-055/P15-062 all extensively iterated on cache eviction, lock bounding, and TTL semantics — but every one of those rounds operated INSIDE the assumption of a single process lifetime. None considered the cross-restart case. r3 P16-033 noticed HANDOFF claimed a non-existent LACERTE_IDEMPOTENCY_TTL_SECONDS env var but explicitly recommended NOT adding any new config — leaving the persistence gap unaddressed. The risk is concrete and high-leverage because WriteDetail (the highest-volume write path per REQUIREMENTS) is append-by-default and the LLM retry-on-error pattern is exactly what README advertises.

verdict.reasoning: Verified the cited code: LacerteSessionManager.cs:152-153 declares `_idempotencyCache` and `_idempotencyLocks` as instance ConcurrentDictionary fields with no serialization, no on-disk shadow log, no startup-restore path. StoreIdempotent at 1900-1904 writes to memory only. Dispose at 2158-2169 only disposes semaphores. The IdempotencyTtl (24h) is wall-clock from process start, not from key issuance, so a restart resets it. Verified the asymmetric danger: WriteDetail at 1149-1230 defaults `replaceIndex=null` and ApplySimDetailWriteWithUndo at 1620+ appends when replaceIndex is null — so re-execution after restart produces duplicate detail rows (the highest-volume write path per REQUIREMENTS). CreateClient (per earlier audits) mints new ClientNumber on every call. Novelty check: searched all 234 prior findings — r1 P14-013/P14-064 (cache eviction), r2 P15-041/P15-055/P15-062 (lock map leak, TTL semantics, cap), r3 P16-033 (env var doc), the r2 TOCTOU race, and the r2 missing env var doc — every single one operates within single-process-lifetime assumptions. title: Idempotency 9102 error leaks 48-bit SHA-256 prefix of cached payload — brute-force oracle for cached PII (SSN/EIN/DOB) on conflict
userOrOpsImpact: An LLM-injected tool call that guesses (or correlates against an operator naming convention like 'intake-<clientID>-ssn') the same idempotencyKey used for a prior write of a sensitive scalar (TaxpayerSSN/C1_15, DOB/C1_19, BankAccountNumber/C1_71, RoutingNumber/C1_72) can iterate guesses on the `value` field and observe `cachedFingerprintPrefix` in each 9102 conflict envelope. Match a 48-bit prefix and the guess equals the cached value. SSN search space is ~30 bits, RoutingNumber ~30 bits (and constrained), DOB ~15 bits — the 48-bit prefix is wider than the search space, so a match is unique. The narrow wire-scope redactor (P15-001) doesn't scrub these context keys, and `reason` survives wire-scope intentionally so the LLM gets diagnostics. Net: an injection-controlled LLM call sequence can extract cached PII from the idempotency cache one secret at a time.
description: P15-074 added `cachedFingerprintPrefix` and `requestedFingerprintPrefix` (first 8 chars of base64 SHA-256, ~48 bits each) to the 9102 IdempotencyConflict context dict to help triage. The keys are not in `_wireRedactionKeys` and they survive `WrapToolHandler` redaction. The cached fingerprint is computed over `{op, args}` where `args` includes the raw `value` for WriteField — so the prefix is a deterministic function of the secret value plus public structural fields (op, table, clientNumber, field, subClientId, stateAbbrev). An attacker who knows or can enumerate everything except `value` (true for any single-scalar write like SSN, DOB, RoutingNumber) brute-forces `value` offline by computing BuildPayload-shape JSON, SHA-256ing, base64-encoding, and comparing the first 8 chars to the leaked prefix. The triage benefit (telling two payloads apart at a glance) is preserved by an HMAC with a process-ephemeral random key — the operator can still distinguish two prefixes within the same session, but cross-process / cross-payload-search-space brute force is foreclosed.
recommendation: Replace SHA-256 prefix with HMAC-SHA-256(process_local_random_key, payload) prefix, where the key is generated once at LacerteSessionManager construction via RandomNumberGenerator and held only in-memory. Same 8-char wire shape, same triage UX (operator sees two distinct prefixes meaning two distinct payloads), but the prefix is no longer a brute-forceable hash of caller-controlled inputs. Alternative fix: drop the two prefix keys from the 9102 context entirely and rely on `existingEntryCreatedAt` + `existingEntryAgeMs` (already present) for triage. Add `cachedFingerprintPrefix` and `requestedFingerprintPrefix` to `_wireRedactionKeys` as a belt-and-suspenders. Either path lands in one file plus the matching tests in LacerteSessionManagerTests.cs:680-681.
rationale: P15-074 introduced the prefix disclosure as a triage convenience; no prior audit round modeled it as an attacker oracle. Grep of all three audit JSONs confirms no finding touches fingerprint disclosure, brute-force oracle, or HMAC keying for idempotency. The threat model the round-4 brief asks about (`SHA-256 fingerprint includes secrets — does cache key get logged anywhere?`) is satisfied: yes, it's logged to the wire envelope via the 9102 context dict, and yes, the secret-search-space is small enough (30-bit SSN, 15-bit DOB) that 48 bits is a unique match. Fix is one file, ~20 LoC including the HMAC key field and BuildPayload changeover. The wire-scope redactor (P15-001) deliberately keeps `reason` and most context keys visible so the LLM can self-diagnose — the prefix keys were added under that same intent without considering the cache-as-oracle angle.

Verified the code: LacerteSessionManager.cs lines 1884-1895 do put `cachedFingerprintPrefix` and `requestedFingerprintPrefix` (8 chars of base64 SHA-256 = 48 bits) into the 9102 IdempotencyConflict context dict. WrapToolHandler.SerializeError (line 179) runs Redact with RedactionScope.Wire, and _wireRedactionKeys (WireLog.cs:230-250) does NOT contain either prefix key — so they DO survive to the wire envelope and reach the LLM. BuildPayload (line 2107) is SHA-256 over `{op, args}` where args includes raw `value` for WriteField — deterministic, no salt, no HMAC key. So the prefix IS a brute-forceable hash of caller-controlled inputs.

Novelty: Grepped all 3 prior audit JSONs for fingerprint/oracle/brute/HMAC. The R1 finding at audit-findings.json:1387 covered the *timing-oracle on String.Equals of the full fingerprint* and was explicitly rejected ("timing-oracle half is essentially a non-issue"). The R2 finding at audit-findings-r2.json:1783 covered the type-mismatch wrong-message branch (the P15-074 work that *introduced* the prefix disclosure). R2 finding at line 368 covered Idempotency telemetry (the P15-016 work). NONE of the prior rounds modeled prefix-as-deterministic-hash-oracle for PII recovery. The threat vector — that 48 bits is wider than SSN's ~30-bit / DOB's ~15-bit search space, making offline brute-force trivially identify cached secrets — is genuinely new in round 4.

Material improvement: The project already invests heavily in wire-scope PII redaction (P14-018, P15-001, P15-019, P15-038) precisely because the LLM cannot be trusted with PII even though it's a single-operator tool. The threat model the project has *already accepted* is "LLM might leak PII it sees." This finding shows that P15-074 inadvertently opened a side channel that's inconsistent with that stance: the LLM doesn't directly see the SSN, but it sees a value from which the SSN is recoverable in seconds via offline brute force given small search space (~30 bits for SSN, ~15 bits for DOB, ~30 bits for routing number which is also CRC-constrained to ~26 bits). The fix is ~20 LoC (HMAC with process-local random key, or just remove the two prefix keys and rely on existingEntryCreatedAt for triage), one file plus one test. Cost-benefit is excellent.

Caveat that softens confidence from "high" to "medium": for the attack to land, the operator must use a guessable/correlatable idempotency key naming convention (e.g., "intake-<clientID>-ssn"), and an attacker must inject the iteration sequence into the LLM. For a personal tool with operator-chosen opaque keys (e.g., GUIDs) the practical exploit window is narrow. But the project's defense-in-depth posture on PII redaction means closing this is consistent with the existing bar, and the fix is so cheap that the cost-benefit holds even at low probability of exploitation.

Preferred (HMAC keying — preserves triage UX): In LacerteSessionManager.cs, add a private static readonly byte[] field initialized once at type construction via RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32). Refactor BuildPayload (line 2107-2124) to use HMACSHA256 keyed with that random key instead of plain SHA256.Create(). The 8-char base64 prefix is still emitted and the operator still sees two distinct prefixes when two distinct payloads collide on a key (preserving the triage UX P15-074 wanted), but the prefix is no longer a public deterministic function of attacker-controllable inputs — offline brute force is foreclosed because the attacker doesn't have the key. Since BuildPayload is also used to populate entry.PayloadFingerprint (line 1884), the in-memory cache lookup at line 1837 (`entry.PayloadFingerprint == payload`) still works because both sides go through the same keyed function within the process. Process-local key is the right scope: cross-restart cache misses are already inevitable (cache is in-memory only), so there's no cross-restart key-rotation problem.

Alternative (drop the prefix keys — zero crypto): Delete `cachedFingerprintPrefix` and `requestedFingerprintPrefix` from the data dict at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1892-1893. title: lacerte_field_write_bulk has no batch-size cap — single MCP call can fan out unbounded N writes with no guardrail
userOrOpsImpact: An LLM constructing a bulk-write payload can hand the tool a 50,000-entry array. There is NO Math.Min, NO Pagination.MaxLimit, NO per-call cap, NO per-row confirmation gate. The tool happily walks the entire array, holding the per-key idempotency lock chain, writing to the live SDK one row at a time. A misclick by the operator ('write zip=12345 for every client in NY' — but the LLM emitted every client in the firm) becomes a multi-thousand-row mutation with one tool call and no chance to inspect before it lands. Compare lacerte_detail_read at DetailsTools.cs:71 which IS bounded by Pagination.MaxLimit=1000. Writes have a much higher blast radius than reads but the inverse guardrail posture.
description: FieldWriteBulkTools.LacerteFieldWriteBulk accepts `BulkWriteEntry[] entries` with no length cap anywhere. The only documented behavior on size is the empty-array no-op note. Pagination.MaxLimit (1000) is the project's existing read-bound constant and would be a natural ceiling. The continueOnError default is now safer (false, per the doc), but the default doesn't help when the LLM's intent — and the entire array — is wrong. There's also no per-batch confirmation primitive: no `confirmIfOver` parameter that forces the LLM to acknowledge an N>100 batch by passing the same number a second time, no `expectedCount` cross-check, no requireDryRunFirst flag.
recommendation: Add a hard cap and a confirmation gate. (1) Cap entries.Length at MaxBulkEntries=500 (or Pagination.MaxLimit=1000); throw a new SyntheticStatusCode 9020 BulkBatchTooLarge with remediation 'Split the batch into chunks of <=500 entries and submit sequentially with a shared idempotencyKey prefix.' This bounds the worst-case blast and forces the LLM to be deliberate. (2) Add an optional `expectedCount` parameter — when supplied, must equal entries.Length or the call throws 9021 BulkBatchCountMismatch. Lets the operator's prompt say 'write to exactly 47 NY clients' and have the system enforce it. (3) Consider a soft warning gate: when entries.Length > 100 AND dryRun==false AND no `acknowledgeLargeBatch: true` flag was set, throw 9022 BulkBatchUnconfirmed with remediation 'Set acknowledgeLargeBatch=true OR rerun with dryRun=true to preview.' Default-deny large blast radius without a deliberate ack. (4) Document the cap in the tool's [Description] so the LLM knows up-front not to fan out beyond the cap.
rationale: Prior rounds (P15-008 created the bulk tool, P16-064 added firstFailureIndex + recoveryHint, P16-026 unified field naming) focused on per-row mechanics and post-failure recovery UX. None addressed the size-of-batch precondition. The cost-of-failure lens specifically asked 'Tools missing per-row confirmation when batch is large (any guardrail at batch > 100?)' — answer is no. The project's own pagination layer (Pagination.MaxLimit=1000) is the obvious precedent the write tool should respect with equal or stricter bounds. Fix is ~15 lines in the existing pre-flight section of the tool, sim-testable, no SDK dependency.

verdict.reasoning: Verified the gap is real: FieldWriteBulkTools.cs accepts BulkWriteEntry[] with zero length validation — the only entries handling is `entries ??= Array.Empty<BulkWriteEntry>();` at line 161, then a straight `for (int i = 0; i < entries.Length; i++)` loop that fans out N writes through the SDK chokepoint. Confirmed via Grep of all three prior audit files (audit-findings.json, audit-findings-r2.json, audit-findings-r3.json) using terms: bulk/batch/cap/MaxLimit/blast/DoS/guardrail/acknowledge/expectedCount/MaxBatch/fan-out — no prior finding addresses the size-of-batch precondition. Prior bulk-tool findings cover naming (P16-026/P16-080), error-code mismatch (P16-063), and recovery envelope (P16-064) but the entries.Length upper bound is genuinely unsurfaced. Material improvement is clear: the project already enforces Pagination.MaxLimit=1000 on every read tool (8 tools verified), so a write tool with strictly higher blast radius having no equivalent ceiling is an asymmetry against the project's own convention. An LLM constructing a bulk-write payload from a fuzzy operator intent has no structural braking today. The hard-cap (recommendation 1) and expectedCount cross-check (recommendation 2) are high-value, sim-testable, ~15 lines in the existing pre-flight section before line 161. Recommendation 3 (acknowledgeLargeBatch flag at >100) is more debatable polish that adds tool surface area; the core cap is the load-bearing part.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add a hard cap on entries.Length in FieldWriteBulkTools.cs pre-flight (before line 161 `entries ??= Array.Empty<BulkWriteEntry>();`). Define `const int MaxBulkEntries = 500;` (or reuse `Pagination.MaxLimit = 1000` — pick stricter since write blast radius > read). Throw a new SyntheticStatusCode 9020 BulkBatchTooLarge with context {entryCount, maxAllowed, table} and remediation: 'Split into chunks of <=500 entries; submit sequentially with a shared idempotencyKey prefix so already-succeeded rows replay from cache.' Add optional `expectedCount` parameter — when non-null, must equal entries.Length or throw 9021 BulkBatchCountMismatch with context {expected, actual}. Update the tool's [Description] string to name the cap so the LLM knows up-front. Skip the soft acknowledgeLargeBatch gate (recommendation 3) — it adds tool-surface complexity without strong evidence the hard cap alone is insufficient; revisit if real misuse occurs. Cover with two simulation tests: (a) entries.Length == MaxBulkEntries + 1 throws 9020 with correct context, (b) expectedCount=10 but entries.Length=11 throws 9021. Document the cap in REGRESSION_CHECKLIST.md write section.

title: InformationalVersion's git-SHA suffix is dead code — neither ci.yml nor release.ps1 sets SourceRevisionId, so the +abc1234 stamp promised by P14-040/status/doctor never fires
line: Directory.Build.props:35 (conditional on $(SourceRevisionId) != ''); ci.yml:47-48 (build step does not pass -p:SourceRevisionId); release.ps1:36 (same)
userOrOpsImpact: An operator hitting a bug in a deployed build runs `lacerte-mcp status` to capture the build stamp for the bug report and sees `"buildVersion": "0.1.0"` with no SHA suffix — there is no way to identify WHICH commit produced this exe. Combined with the non-deterministic byte issue (separate finding), this means a bug report can never be traced back to source. The Directory.Build.props comment 'CI fills SourceRevisionId' is a lie — CI does not fill it, release.ps1 does not fill it, and no MSBuild target in the repo populates it. The InformationalVersion attribute that lands in the compiled assembly is always the fallback `0.1.0` value (the second InformationalVersion line, condition `'$(InformationalVersion)' == ''`).
description: Directory.Build.props:35 reads `<InformationalVersion Condition="'$(SourceRevisionId)' != '' AND $(SourceRevisionId.Length) >= 7">$(Version)+$(SourceRevisionId.Substring(0,7))</InformationalVersion>` with a fallback at line 36. But $(SourceRevisionId) is NOT a built-in MSBuild property — it is populated by either (a) the Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub package (or any SourceLink provider) via its InitializeSourceControlInformation target, (b) an explicit `dotnet build -p:SourceRevisionId=$GITHUB_SHA`, (c) a custom git-rev-parse target. Verified: no SourceLink PackageReference anywhere (Grep for `SourceLink`/`GitInfo`/`MinVer`/`Nerdbank` finds only the negative comment in Directory.Build.props). ci.yml line 47 reads `dotnet build LacertMCP.sln -c Debug -p:Platform=x64 --no-restore` — no -p:SourceRevisionId. release.ps1 line 36 reads `& $script:Dotnet build $script:Solution -c Release -p:Platform=x64 -nologo` — same. The test at src/LacertMCP.Tests/Cli/StatusCommandTests.cs:225-229 even hedges with a comment 'SourceRevisionId may be empty in some dev builds' — but it's empty in ALL builds because no path populates it. Result: the BuildInfo.Version that `lacerte_session_status` / `lacerte-mcp doctor` / `lacerte-mcp status` print is always `0.1.0` flat, never `0.1.0+abc1234`, and the operator has no commit-level forensic anchor.
recommendation: Two-line fix, both targeted at the actual build entry points. (1) In `.github/workflows/ci.yml` Build step (line 47, both jobs): change the command to `dotnet build LacertMCP.sln -c Debug -p:Platform=x64 -p:SourceRevisionId=${{ github.sha }} --no-restore`. (2) In `scripts/release.ps1` line 36: change to `& $script:Dotnet build $script:Solution -c Release -p:Platform=x64 -p:SourceRevisionId=$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>$null) -nologo`. Wrap the git call in try/catch to fall back to empty string if not in a git repo (preserves current behavior for sim/non-git contexts). Optionally also add a Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub PackageReference to Directory.Build.props with PrivateAssets=all, which auto-populates SourceRevisionId via the InitializeSourceControlInformation target AND adds repo+commit metadata to the PDB for go-to-definition from a deployed exe — but the two-line build-arg fix is the minimum viable. Add a positive regression test to StatusCommandTests that uses Process.Start to exec `lacerte-mcp status --json -p:SourceRevisionId=deadbeefcafe1234` and asserts the output buildVersion contains `+deadbee` (matches the substring-7 logic in Directory.Build.props:35). Update the dead-code comment in Directory.Build.props lines 30-34 to match the new reality.
rationale: P14-040 added the version stamping infrastructure (Directory.Build.props lines 26-37) and the BuildInfoTests guardrail (BuildInfoTests.cs), but neither verified that the SourceRevisionId-driven SHA suffix actually populates in any build path. P14-009 added CI but did not wire SourceRevisionId. P14-039 added scripts/release.ps1 but did not wire SourceRevisionId either. The three pieces were each landed in isolation and never integration-tested — the comment 'CI fills SourceRevisionId' in Directory.Build.props was an assumption that never came true. No prior finding in any of the 234 catches this. The StatusCommandTests negative-test ('we don't assert presence of `+` because SourceRevisionId may be empty in some dev builds') is the smoking-gun acknowledgment that this is broken — the comment papers over what should be a real assertion.

Verified directly against the three cited files. (1) C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/Directory.Build.props line 35 reads `<InformationalVersion Condition="'$(SourceRevisionId)' != '' AND $(SourceRevisionId.Length) >= 7">$(Version)+$(SourceRevisionId.Substring(0,7))</InformationalVersion>` with a fallback at line 36 — confirmed. The comment on lines 30-34 promises "CI fills SourceRevisionId". (2) .github/workflows/ci.yml line 48 runs `dotnet build LacertMCP.sln -c Debug -p:Platform=x64 --no-restore` — no `-p:SourceRevisionId=${{ github.sha }}` argument anywhere in either of the two jobs (windows-build-test and ubuntu-build-smoke). (3) scripts/release.ps1 line 36 runs `& $script:Dotnet build $script:Solution -c Release -p:Platform=x64 -nologo` — no SourceRevisionId either. (4) A repo-wide Grep for `SourceRevisionId|SourceLink|InitializeSourceControlInformation` returns hits only in Directory.Build.props, the StatusCommandTests, the audit-findings JSONs, and the Todo.md — confirming no SourceLink/MinVer/Nerdbank/GitInfo package and no custom MSBuild target populates SourceRevisionId. So $(SourceRevisionId) is empty in EVERY build path that the repo ships — local dev, CI, and release.ps1.

Novelty check: searched audit-findings.json, -r2.json, -r3.json for `SourceRevisionId`, `github.sha`, `git rev-parse`, `SourceLink`, `InitializeSourceControlInformation`. Prior hits cluster around (a) P14-040 (original P14-040 finding which CREATED the broken Directory.Build.props with the same Substring expression, recommended SourceRevisionId as the data source but never wired it from CI/release), and (b) P16-068 (r3, escaped-`+` in `status --json`), which assumed the `+abc1234` suffix is actually produced and only fixed the JSON encoder. The current state produces `0.1.0` flat across every channel (dev, CI, release zips), making the entire status/doctor/buildVersion surface forensically useless for the exact "operator pastes status into a bug report" workflow described in the project's CLAUDE.md (single-operator personal tool). Both `github.sha` and `git rev-parse HEAD` are reliable in their contexts. Also the negative test in StatusCommandTests should be flipped to a positive assertion once the data source is wired — closes the test-as-papering-over-bug loop. Cost: ~3 lines of YAML/PS plus 1 test, in-session actionable, no Lacerte/Windows dependency.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:

Line 48 (windows-build-test Build step) and line 92 (ubuntu-build-smoke Build step): change `dotnet build LacertMCP.sln -c Debug -p:Platform=x64 --no-restore` to `dotnet build LacertMCP.sln -c Debug -p:Platform=x64 -p:SourceRevisionId=${{ github.sha }} --no-restore`. The `github.sha` context value is always the 40-char commit SHA on both push and pull_request triggers — the Substring(0,7) guard in Directory.Build.props will trim it.

2. scripts/release.ps1 line 36 — wrap the git call so non-git contexts (a hand-unzip of the source) still work:

try { $gitSha = (& git rev-parse HEAD 2>$null).Trim() } catch { $gitSha = '' }
$buildArgs = @('build', $script:Solution, '-c', 'Release', '-p:Platform=x64', '-nologo')

3. src/LacertMCP.Tests/Cli/StatusCommandTests.cs lines 218-230 — flip the hedge into a positive guardrail by adding a sibling test that runs StatusCommand against a synthetic assembly whose AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute contains a `+`. Also update the comment on StatusCommandTests.cs:227-229 to reflect the new reality — "build hash is omitted in dev builds without -p:SourceRevisionId; CI populates it via github.sha".

4. Directory.Build.props lines 30-34 — replace the misleading "CI fills SourceRevisionId" comment with the actual contract: "Populated by ci.yml (`-p:SourceRevisionId=${{ github.sha }}`) and scripts/release.ps1 (`git rev-parse HEAD`). Local `dotnet build` without that arg produces the bare $(Version) fallback — intentional for non-git contexts (sim/tarball)."

Out of scope for this fix (but worth a follow-up note): adding Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub as a PackageReference with PrivateAssets=all would auto-populate SourceRevisionId everywhere via the InitializeSourceControlInformation target AND embed repo+commit metadata in PDBs (enabling go-to-definition from deployed binaries). But for a single-operator personal tool the two-line build-arg fix is the minimum viable and matches the project's "no overkill" DECISIONS posture.

title: ValidateLogDir allowlist silently disables itself on POSIX — `LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH=/etc/cron.d` passes the same gate that blocks `C:\Windows\System32` on Windows
userOrOpsImpact: An LLM (or test fixture, or shell rc) that sets a hostile LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH on Linux/macOS — the project's explicitly-supported simulation dev environment — gets the directory provisioned anywhere the process can write (system dirs, /etc/cron.d, another user's home). On Windows the same input is rejected. The XML doc + the operator-facing P14-049 design promise an allowlist of {USERPROFILE, TEMP, LACERTE_DATA_ROOT} — on POSIX none of those env vars are conventionally populated (POSIX uses HOME and TMPDIR, not USERPROFILE/TEMP/TMP), so the `roots.Count == 0` branch fires and returns `canonical` unconditionally. The inline comment claims 'Operator-controlled env on real boxes always populates USERPROFILE + TEMP' — that is true for Windows boxes only, and is false for the Linux/macOS sim-mode dev boxes the project explicitly supports.
description: ValidateLogDir builds its allowlist from four env vars that are all Windows conventions — USERPROFILE, TEMP, TMP, LACERTE_DATA_ROOT. On Linux/macOS none of the first three are populated by default (POSIX uses HOME / TMPDIR / XDG_RUNTIME_DIR), and LACERTE_DATA_ROOT is only set when the operator explicitly chose a Lacerte install root — which a sim-mode dev box typically has not. With zero roots discovered, the code at line 219-226 returns the canonical path verbatim with the comment 'permit canonical path as-is. Operator-controlled env on real boxes always populates USERPROFILE + TEMP, so this branch is just a no-op for tests.' That assumption is false off-Windows. Combined with WireLog.ResolveConfig (line 1204) using the returned path verbatim and then Directory.CreateDirectory + opening a writer there, an attacker-controlled (or LLM-typo'd) LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH writes the lacerte-YYYYMMDD.log files into arbitrary filesystem locations. The same input '/etc/cron.d' is silently accepted on Linux but rejected on Windows — defeating both the boundary invariant 'sim and live observationally identical' and the P14-049 threat model. The CLAUDE.md operating system explicitly designates POSIX as the dev-mode runtime.
recommendation: Either (a) treat 'no roots discovered' as REJECT instead of permit (returning null forces WireLog to fall back to ./logs/, which is always safe), with a one-line ILogger warning so operators know their LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH was overridden; or (b) add the POSIX-conventional roots (HOME, TMPDIR, XDG_CACHE_HOME, /tmp) to the TryAddRoot list so the allowlist is actually populated on Linux/macOS. Option (a) is the safer fail-closed default and matches WireLog's never-throw-just-fall-back policy. Pin with one new PathValidation test asserting that on an env dict with only POSIX-shaped vars (HOME, TMPDIR) ValidateLogDir('/etc/cron.d') returns null, not a canonical path. Update the inline comment at line 221-224 to reflect actual behavior.
rationale: Audit-findings r1 task 'dataPath path-traversal / write-outside-expected-root not validated' (audit-findings.json:1059) drove the original creation of the gate; r2/r3 did not revisit cross-platform allowlist coverage. No prior finding examines what happens to ValidateLogDir specifically when run off-Windows. The boundary invariant 'sim and live observationally identical' explicitly covers this case but the implementation diverges.

verdict.reasoning: Code claim verified: PathValidation.cs:204-226 builds the allowlist exclusively from Windows-conventional env vars (USERPROFILE, TEMP, TMP, LACERTE_DATA_ROOT) and falls through to `return canonical;` when roots.Count==0. The existing test ValidateLogDir_NoEnvAllowlistRoots_ReturnsCanonical (SessionToolsTests.cs:342-351) explicitly blesses this behavior with the comment "Production env always has USERPROFILE on Windows so the allowlist is real there" — which encodes the very assumption that breaks on POSIX. On Linux/macOS none of USERPROFILE/TEMP/TMP are populated by default (POSIX convention is HOME/TMPDIR/XDG_*), so a LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH override of /etc/cron.d would be accepted off-Windows while C:\Windows\System32 would be rejected on-Windows — a direct violation of the project's "sim and live observationally identical" boundary invariant from CLAUDE.md. WireLog.cs:1204 consumes the result verbatim and then Directory.CreateDirectory + writes log files there. Novelty confirmed: grepped audit-findings.json/r2.json/r3.json for ValidateLogDir/LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH/POSIX/HOME/TMPDIR/cross-platform/allowlist — P14-049 (r1) created the gate, r2/r3 never revisited its cross-platform coverage; r3 task P16-065/066 only touched WireLog observability, not the validator allowlist. Material improvement is medium-confidence: the threat (env-controlled LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH) requires an actor who already has substantial process control, and this is a single-operator personal tool — so the "security" framing is overstated. But the underlying defect is a real correctness/consistency gap: a defensive gate that the project deliberately invested in (P14-049) silently no-ops on the platform the project explicitly supports for development, and the inline comment misrepresents the actual behavior. The fail-closed fix (return null when roots.Count==0, log one-line warning, let WireLog fall back to ./logs) is ~5 LOC and one new test — cheap enough that closing the boundary-invariant divergence is worth it even at modest impact.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Adopt option (a) — fail-closed when no allowlist roots are discovered — rather than option (b) — because adding POSIX roots (HOME, TMPDIR, XDG_CACHE_HOME, /tmp) silently widens the surface and an operator who set LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH=/etc/cron.d on Linux probably also has HOME set, so /home/user/.config/whatever-anchored paths would still pass even though that wasn't the operator's intent. Fail-closed is the cleaner match for WireLog's never-throw-just-fall-back policy. Concrete edit in PathValidation.cs:219-226: change `return canonical;` to `return null;` and update the comment to "No allowlist roots available — reject so WireLog falls back to its CWD-relative default ./logs instead of provisioning arbitrary filesystem locations. Operators who need a custom log path must populate USERPROFILE or LACERTE_DATA_ROOT explicitly." Update ValidateLogDir_NoEnvAllowlistRoots_ReturnsCanonical in SessionToolsTests.cs to assert null (rename test to ValidateLogDir_NoEnvAllowlistRoots_RejectsToForceFallback). Add a new test ValidateLogDir_PosixShapedEnv_RejectsArbitraryPath that passes an env dict with only {HOME, TMPDIR} populated and asserts ValidateLogDir("/etc/cron.d") returns null. Add a single ILogger.LogInformation in WireLog.ResolveConfig:1204 when validated==null and dirOverride was non-empty, so an operator who set LACERTE_DEBUG_LOG_PATH and got silent fallback can discover why (the existing P16-065/066 lacerte_session_status surfacing of wireLogPath will then show the fallback ./logs path, closing the diagnostic loop). Out of scope: do NOT add POSIX env vars to TryAddRoot — the operator-on-POSIX use case is satisfied by LACERTE_DATA_ROOT which they're already expected to set in sim-mode config; avoiding HOME keeps the allowlist intentional rather than permissive-by-default.

title: Read-tool response row keys ship PascalCase ClientNumber/SubClientID/StateAbbrev — wire keys disagree with the canonical camelCase tool params P16 just enforced
line: 1736-1749 (CloneRow), reached via ReadClient (line 698), ReadTable/ReadTableCore (line 782), ReadSubclients (called at line 788+)
userOrOpsImpact: Every row that comes back from lacerte_client_read, lacerte_client_list, lacerte_table_read, lacerte_subclient_read, lacerte_states_read, lacerte_state_subs_read, etc. ships JSON keys `ClientNumber`, `SubClientID`, and `StateAbbrev` (and inside Fields, `ClientID`) — but the SAME tool's input parameters and filter args were just canonicalized in round-3 P16 to camelCase `clientNumber`, `subClientId`, `stateAbbrev`. An LLM that calls `lacerte_table_read(stateAbbrev="CA")` and then writes a filter `row.stateAbbrev === "CA"` against the response will get `undefined` on every row; the actual key is `row.StateAbbrev`. This is the second-most-confusing failure mode in a tool surface (after wrong-tool-name errors): the wire emits and accepts both casings for the same concept, in the same response envelope.
description: CloneRow at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1736-1749 builds the row dictionaries that ALL sim-mode reads return to the MCP wire. It hard-codes three top-level keys as PascalCase: `["ClientNumber"]`, `["SubClientID"]`, `["StateAbbrev"]`. Then it copies `src.Fields` verbatim, which includes `["ClientID"]` (set by SimulationStore.cs:556 / SimulationStore.Seed.cs:85,153,196) and a slew of FoxPro PascalCase column names (`C1_0`...). These dictionaries are returned as `client = row` / `clients = page.Rows` / `rows = ...` by the tools. WrapToolHandler.JsonOptions has no PropertyNamingPolicy AND System.Text.Json's CamelCase policy would NOT fix this anyway: the policy normalizes class/anonymous-object property names but writes Dictionary<string,object?> keys verbatim. So the round-3 P16-084 recommendation ("add CamelCase JsonNamingPolicy") that the prior verdict thought would clean up wire casing will leave these row keys untouched. Round 3's P16-054 / P16-084 / P16-061-062 covered casing drift in *tool parameter names*, *SessionMode strings*, and *EF-status column aliases* — none of them flagged that the read-row dictionaries themselves still ship the pre-canonicalization PascalCase. The drift is now structurally locked-in by CloneRow being a single chokepoint that ships the wrong shape.
recommendation: Two-line fix in CloneRow plus matching seed-data fix. (1) In LacerteSessionManager.cs:1740-1743, change the three top-level keys to canonical camelCase: `["clientNumber"]`, `["subClientId"]`, `["stateAbbrev"]`. (2) In SimulationStore.cs:556 and SimulationStore.Seed.cs:85,153,196 change `["ClientID"]` to `["clientId"]` so the row.Fields copy through CloneRow also surfaces camelCase. (3) Update the StatesTools/SubclientsTools [Description] strings that mention `(ClientNumber, SubClientID, StateAbbrev)` to use the canonical casing too — they currently teach the LLM the wrong shape. (4) Add one regression test in a new `WireCasingTests.cs` that calls each read tool and asserts every key in the returned row matches `^[a-z]` OR matches the DBF column allowlist regex `^C[1-9]_\d+$` (FoxPro columns are intentionally preserved). This guards every future tool addition automatically. The DBF column names (C1_0, C1_1, FilingStatus, etc.) stay as-is — those are the source-of-truth Lacerte field codes and have to ship verbatim; the finding is specifically about the three SDK-meta keys CloneRow injects. Sim-mode-verifiable in ~30 minutes, no live dependency, no breaking change for the operator beyond what P16-084 already proposes.
rationale: Distinct from r3 P16-054 / P16-084 (parameter-name casing — input side only), r3 P16-061/P16-062 (SessionMode enum string casing), r3 P16-053 (origin field vocabulary), and r2 P15-061 (EF-status column aliases). Those all flagged casing on either tool-param inputs or specific named columns; none looked at the row-dictionary construction site that's the chokepoint for nearly every read tool's output keys. Verified by grep across all 234 prior findings — `CloneRow` is only referenced in audit-findings.json:304 in the context of full-DBF cloning for pagination cost, never for the casing of the keys it emits. The novel observation is the structural one: P16-084's CamelCase JsonNamingPolicy fix would not normalize Dictionary keys, so the prior round's intended cleanup leaves this exact drift live on the wire.
